title: 3-Read Friday #12: Variation Theory, Unit Planning, and Teacher Knowledge
author: Craig Barton
summary: Craig Barton's 3-Read Friday #12 curates three posts on curriculum theory and planning practice. Christian Moore Anderson clarifies what Variation Theory actually asks of teachers, cautioning against simply presenting examples and non-examples and instead arguing for deliberately drawing students' attention to the critical features that change between them. Dylan Kane describes why unit-level planning, not lesson-level planning, is where his most valuable planning time goes, since it is the unit that determines coherence, practice, and engagement across several weeks of instruction. Dan Meyer draws a distinction between subject-matter knowledge and knowledge of student misconceptions, arguing the latter is the more powerful and more neglected form of teacher expertise. Barton links the three as different angles on the same idea: good teaching depends on deliberately structured knowledge, whether that knowledge belongs to the curriculum designer or the teacher.
points: Variation Theory is not simply showing examples and non-examples; it requires deliberately focusing on what changes between them so students' attention lands on the critical features.
Dylan Kane's most valuable planning time is spent at the unit level, where coherence, built-in practice, and engagement across several weeks get decided -- not in individual lesson plans.

Dan Meyer's research citation shows teachers had strong subject-matter knowledge (84.5% correct) but weak knowledge of common student misconceptions (42.7% identified), and only the combination of both predicted real student gains.

Barton's selections converge on a single idea: whether it's a curriculum designer sequencing a unit or a teacher anticipating a wrong answer, good teaching depends on deliberately structured knowledge.
quotes: Regular readers will know what a massive fan of Variation Theory I am.

He cautions against simply showing a series of examples and non-examples, and instead makes the case for initially focussing on differences, considering carefully what changes we can make to draw our students’ attention to the critical features.
If Dylan’s post had been around back then, I could have saved myself (and my students) a lot of pain!
I have found this approach leads to more coherent lessons, and allows me to be more flexible as I am not tied to trying to cover each idea within the confines of 50 minutes.
Dan draws the important distinction between knowing your subject and knowing how to teach your subject, and how a teacher's awareness of where students are likely to struggle can improve the latter.
